---
title: "Checking a linear regression"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

A **regression check** compares a model prediction with an observable pattern. Passing such a check cannot certify the model as true; a useful check instead helps us locate failures that matter for the linguistic comparison.

The checked response is the [aggregated Provo word position measure](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data): mean log first fixation duration among retained positive fixations. The predictor is modeled cloze surprisal, the negative base 2 logarithm of the fitted cloze probability defined in that discussion. These plots can expose failures across positions and passages, but the table contains neither skipped reader outcomes nor residual patterns for individual readers.

Recall that a [residual](residuals.qmd) is observed minus fitted response. Residual plots compare those discrepancies with patterns predicted by the fitted model; they do not observe the population errors directly.

We proceed restriction by restriction: first the conditional-mean shape and passage structure, then residual spread and tail shape, and finally the limits on repairs supported by the aggregated table.

We check three restrictions: (i) a straight conditional mean, (ii) stable residual location across passages, and (iii) approximately normal residuals for conventional finite sample inference.

The basic idea is to translate each mathematical restriction into a pattern that we could have observed. A straight conditional mean predicts no systematic bend in residuals. A common passage location predicts that passage-average residuals fluctuate around zero rather than remaining shifted together. A normal error model predicts a particular relation between ordered residuals and normal quantiles. We will inspect those consequences separately, because one display cannot diagnose every restriction at once.

Here a **quantile** is a cutoff that leaves a stated proportion of a distribution below it. A normal quantile plot pairs the smallest observed residual with a low normal quantile, the next residual with the next quantile, and so on. If the shapes agree, the pairs tend to fall near a straight line.

Each restriction predicts an observable pattern. If the straight mean is adequate, a smooth of residuals against surprisal should tend to remain near zero. If passage location is adequately represented, average residuals for each passage should tend to fluctuate around zero without stable passage shifts. If the Gaussian tail approximation is adequate for conventional inference, ordered residuals should tend to follow a straight normal quantile reference. These are model predictions rather than visual certification rules.

## Linear form and passage structure

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-diagnostic-models
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)

linear_fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
quadratic_fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c + I(cloze_surprisal_c^2),
  data = provo
)
provo$linear_fitted <- fitted(linear_fit)
provo$linear_residual <- residuals(linear_fit)

passage_residuals <- aggregate(
  linear_residual ~ Text_ID,
  data = provo,
  FUN = mean
)

data.frame(
  model = c("linear", "quadratic diagnostic"),
  r_squared = c(
    summary(linear_fit)$r.squared,
    summary(quadratic_fit)$r.squared
  ),
  residual_sd = c(
    summary(linear_fit)$sigma,
    summary(quadratic_fit)$sigma
  )
)
```

Adding the squared observed predictor changes $R^2$ from `r sprintf("%.4f", summary(linear_fit)$r.squared)` to `r sprintf("%.4f", summary(quadratic_fit)$r.squared)`. The added term relaxes the straight line restriction, so the change measures how costly that restriction is in the observed position summaries. Establishing a quadratic processing mechanism would additionally require a measurement and experimental argument linking the squared term to that process.

To see the added flexibility, compare $m(x)=a+bx$ with $m(x)=a+bx+cx^2$. In the first expression, every one-unit step changes the mean by $b$. In the second, the change from $x$ to $x+1$ is $b+c(2x+1)$, which can differ across the predictor range. The squared term therefore supplies one controlled bend; it does not tell us why that bend arose.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-linear-quadratic-check
#| fig-cap: "Provo positions with the linear fit in blue and the quadratic diagnostic in black."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
grid$linear <- predict(linear_fit, newdata = grid)
grid$quadratic <- predict(quadratic_fit, newdata = grid)

point_opacity <- 0.18
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = linear), color = "#2C6E9B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = quadratic), color = "black", linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-passage-residual-locations
#| fig-cap: "Mean residual for each Provo passage, ordered from lowest to highest."
passage_residuals <- passage_residuals[
  order(passage_residuals$linear_residual),
]
passage_residuals$ordered_passage <- seq_len(nrow(passage_residuals))

ggplot(passage_residuals, aes(ordered_passage, linear_residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(color = "#2C6E9B", size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Passage, ordered by mean residual", y = "Passage mean residual") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The passage means show location differences that the single line does not represent. Their ordering is descriptive; the plot does not treat adjacent ranks as linguistically adjacent passages.

## Residual shape

If the normal working model were exact, ordered standardized residuals would track normal quantiles. A quantile plot makes tail departures visible without reducing the check to one test statistic.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-normal-quantiles
#| fig-cap: "Normal quantiles against ordered Provo regression residuals. The line passes through the empirical quartiles."
n <- nrow(provo)
qq_data <- data.frame(
  normal_quantile = qnorm((seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n),
  ordered_residual = sort(provo$linear_residual)
)
sample_quartiles <- quantile(provo$linear_residual, c(.25, .75))
normal_quartiles <- qnorm(c(.25, .75))
qq_slope <- diff(sample_quartiles) / diff(normal_quartiles)
qq_intercept <- sample_quartiles[[1]] - qq_slope * normal_quartiles[[1]]

qq_opacity <- 0.45
ggplot(qq_data, aes(normal_quantile, ordered_residual)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey50", alpha = qq_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = qq_slope,
    intercept = qq_intercept,
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(x = "Normal quantile", y = "Ordered residual") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The checks point to modest curvature and some tail departure. They do not repair passage or reader dependence. This limit matters: changing the mean function cannot recreate a missing sampling unit.

The quadratic is a low-dimensional probe because it asks whether one additional smooth bend captures a systematic departure from the line. Selecting it as the preferred repair would require a declared target and a held-out or otherwise complexity-aware comparison, as developed for [predictive loss](../model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.qmd). A scale-location plot would probe changing spread rather than curvature; residuals against each predictor would probe whether the failure is localized in the predictor space.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which restriction does the quadratic diagnostic probe?
2. Why is a better in-sample $R^2$ not enough to select the quadratic model?
3. What pattern would an exact normal residual model predict in the quantile plot?
4. Which dependence problem survives both checks?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The quadratic diagnostic probes the straight-line restriction on the conditional mean by allowing a squared surprisal term. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Adding a parameter cannot by itself establish a processing mechanism, and in-sample fit does not measure new-passage performance or account for complexity. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The ordered residuals would track the reference line across the center and tails, apart from ordinary sampling fluctuation. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Passage dependence remains, and missing dependence among responses from the same reader cannot be checked or repaired from the aggregated table. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next use [leverage](leverage-and-influence.qmd) to ask which observed predictor positions have unusual capacity to affect the line.
